label: MLIR / TVM / XLA 与编译器生态

questions.subtopic: XLA / HLO — semantics of a matmul-add fragment
questions.learningObjective: Read a small HLO fragment and identify the semantics of ops, layouts, and reductions.
questions.stem: Consider the following HLO fragment. Which statement about its semantics is correct?

options.text: It computes an elementwise product `A * B` broadcasted to a rank-3 tensor; the `contracting_dims` clause is a display hint and does not affect the arithmetic since HLO's `dot` is always elementwise.
It computes `r = A @ B + C` where `A @ B` contracts axis 1 of A with axis 0 of B (a standard matmul), producing an f32[128,64] result; the trailing `add` is elementwise bias/skip addition.
The `add(d, C)` operation forces `d` and `C` to be broadcast to a common rank-3 shape f32[128,64,1] before summing; HLO does not permit rank-2 elementwise `add`.

The `ROOT` keyword indicates that `r` will be recomputed on every call because it names the output; HLO uses `ROOT` as a re-materialization hint for memory planning, not a semantic marker of the entry return value.

assumptions: Standard HLO / StableHLO semantics as documented.

questions.subtopic: IREE / MLIR-based end-to-end compiler + runtime
questions.learningObjective: Understand IREE's overall architecture: an MLIR-based compiler that produces a bytecode module executed by IREE's runtime.
questions.stem: Which statement about IREE's architecture is correct?

options.text: IREE is a pure Python interpreter for StableHLO IR; it does not perform ahead-of-time compilation and has no separate runtime binary.
IREE targets only mobile/edge deployment; it has no support for server-class GPUs like NVIDIA A100/H100 and cannot use MLIR dialects beyond `tosa`.
IREE is a runtime wrapper around cuBLAS/cuDNN; the 'compilation' step consists of choosing which library kernel to invoke for each op, with no MLIR pipeline in between.

IREE is an MLIR-based compiler that lowers input IR (StableHLO / linalg / tosa) through target-specific pipelines and produces a serialized VM module (`.vmfb`) plus device-specific artifacts; the IREE runtime loads the module and dispatches host and device work through a HAL abstraction supporting CPU / Vulkan / CUDA / Metal / ROCm backends.

assumptions: IREE 2024+ architecture as documented on iree.dev.

questions.subtopic: IREE / Compiler-runtime separation and edge deployment
questions.learningObjective: Understand why IREE separates compiler and runtime and how this enables edge and cross-target deployment.
questions.stem: Which statement best captures the reason IREE cleanly separates its compiler and runtime?

options.text: The separation is purely for internal code organization; end users must run both the compiler and the runtime on the target device at every model invocation, since IREE bytecode cannot be executed without the compiler.
The runtime is only used for testing during development; production deployments must re-implement the runtime themselves because IREE does not distribute a production runtime binary.

The compiler is a heavyweight AOT tool that produces a compact, self-describing artifact; the runtime is a small embeddable library that can be linked into edge/mobile apps without shipping the full MLIR toolchain, enabling deployment where the target device lacks the resources or licensing to host a full compiler.
IREE compiler and runtime share the same binary at deployment; the 'compiler-runtime separation' is a marketing term and has no impact on the artifact structure or edge deployment story.

assumptions: IREE deployment model as documented on iree.dev.

questions.subtopic: MLIR / Affine dialect — affine maps, integer sets, loop nests
questions.learningObjective: Reason about MLIR affine dialect semantics: what makes a loop-nest 'affine' and what transformations rely on that structure.
questions.stem: Consider the following two loop-nest fragments; which statement about their status in the MLIR `affine` dialect is correct?

options.text: Fragment 2 is valid affine IR because `%kidx` is materialized before the inner loop via `arith.index_cast`, and by that point in the SSA order it is treated as a symbolic constant by the affine verifier.

Both fragments are valid affine IR because both use `affine.for` and `affine.load/store`; the affine dialect verifier is deliberately syntactic and does not enforce affine constraints on values used as bounds.
Fragment 1 is invalid because the inner load `%A[%i, %j + 1]` uses a non-trivial affine expression `%j + 1`; affine.load only accepts single-IV indices.

Fragment 1 is valid affine IR because loop bounds, steps, and index expressions are affine functions of loop IVs and symbolic constants (`%N`, `%M`). Fragment 2 is invalid because the inner loop's upper bound (`%kidx`) is a data-dependent value not a symbol, violating the affine dialect's structural requirement.

assumptions: Standard upstream MLIR affine dialect verifier.

questions.subtopic: MLIR / Dialect Conversion, Conversion Target, Type Converter
questions.learningObjective: Understand the roles of Conversion Target, Type Converter, and legalization patterns in an MLIR Dialect Conversion, including the difference between partial and full conversion.
questions.stem: You want to convert `func.func` bodies containing `arith.addi` on `i32` to an `llvm.func` using LLVM Dialect. You configure a `ConversionTarget` marking `LLVMDialect` as legal, `arith.addi` as illegal, register conversion patterns, and set a `TypeConverter` mapping `i32 → i32`. Which statement about the resulting Dialect Conversion is correct?

options.text: Because `arith.addi` is marked illegal, the framework silently deletes any matched op without a rewriter pattern; illegal ops without patterns are simply dropped, and the surrounding IR is left in an inconsistent state that a later Canonicalizer pass must repair.
`applyPartialConversion` requires the same completeness as full conversion; the difference between partial and full is only whether the transformation runs in a single or multiple passes.

Under `applyFullConversion`, every operation in the input (including `func.func`, `func.return`, and `arith.addi`) must have a matching legalization pattern; if any remaining op is not marked legal by the target, the conversion fails with a verification error.

The `TypeConverter` is optional whenever conversion patterns keep types unchanged; here `i32 → i32` is an identity mapping, so registering the TypeConverter has no effect and can be omitted entirely regardless of how the func signature is rewritten.

assumptions: The reader is using upstream MLIR's `applyFullConversion` / `applyPartialConversion` APIs.
`arith.addi` on `i32` has a registered pattern lowering to `llvm.add` on `i32`.

questions.subtopic: MLIR / Dialect, Trait, Interface
questions.learningObjective: Explain the roles of Dialect, Trait, and Interface in MLIR extensibility, and identify what each entity does and does not do.
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about MLIR Dialects, Traits, and Interfaces are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A Trait is compile-time metadata attached to an Op class that Pass writers can query with a static check (e.g., `SameOperandsAndResultType`, `MemoryEffects`), letting analyses and rewrites treat many Ops uniformly.
An Interface is a virtual method table on Ops (or Dialects/Types), letting client code call polymorphic behavior on an Op without knowing its concrete class (e.g., `InferShapedTypeOpInterface`).

Once an Op is defined in one Dialect, it can never be aliased into another Dialect; therefore lowering between Dialects always requires cloning the Op and rebuilding all its uses from scratch, without leveraging any interface polymorphism.
A Dialect is a registration namespace grouping related Operations, Types, and Attributes; different Dialects can coexist in one IRModule, enabling progressive lowering across levels of abstraction.

assumptions: The reader is thinking about MLIR core extensibility mechanisms, not any downstream project's naming.

questions.subtopic: MLIR / GPU dialect — kernel launch, memory space, workgroup semantics
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an MLIR `gpu.launch_func` and identify how the GPU dialect represents grid/block dimensions and memory spaces.
questions.stem: Consider the MLIR fragment below. Which statement about the `gpu.launch_func` and the callee `@kernel` is correct?

options.text: The `kernel` attribute on `gpu.func` is redundant when a `gpu.launch_func` refers to it; removing it would still produce a valid kernel launch, and `%bid * blockDim` is automatically computed by `gpu.block_id x` under the hood.

The launch spawns exactly 4 threads because `blocks in (4, 1, 1)` sets the total thread count; the `threads in` clause is a lowering hint that the NVVM backend may ignore, and memory space 1 denotes shared memory on NVVM targets.

The launch spawns 4 blocks × 256 threads = 1024 threads; `%arg` in memory space 1 (global) is captured as a kernel argument; `gpu.thread_id x` and `gpu.block_id x` give per-thread coordinates, and the bug in the kernel is that `%idx = %bid + %tid` should be `%bid * blockDim + %tid` — as written, indices repeat across blocks and only the first 256 elements are read.
`gpu.launch_func` cannot pass `memref` arguments; only scalars and raw `!llvm.ptr` are permitted, so the IR is invalid and would fail verification before lowering to NVVM.

assumptions: Standard upstream MLIR `gpu` dialect and `gpu-to-nvvm`/`gpu-to-rocdl` lowering conventions.
Memory space integers follow the gpu-dialect convention (0 = global, 3 = workgroup/shared, 5 = private on NVVM lowering).

questions.subtopic: MLIR / Linalg Dialect, generic ops, iterator types
questions.learningObjective: Read a `linalg.generic` op and identify which iterator types encode parallel vs reduction dimensions, and how indexing maps drive the semantics.
questions.stem: Consider the following `linalg.generic` op operating on `%A: tensor<MxKxf32>`, `%B: tensor<KxNxf32>`, `%C: tensor<MxNxf32>`. Which statement describes what this op computes?

options.text: It computes `C[m,n] += A[m,k] * B[k,n]` — a standard matrix multiplication with accumulation into `%C`. The `k` dimension is a reduction iterator, so contributions across `k` are summed; `m` and `n` are parallel iterators.
It computes `C[m,n] = A[m,k] * B[k,n]` for a single arbitrary `k` chosen at runtime because there is no explicit `linalg.reduce` marker inside the region body.
It computes elementwise `C[m,n] = A[m,n] * B[m,n] + C[m,n]`; the indexing maps are ignored by `linalg.generic` and only the region body determines the operation.
It computes a batched matmul across three parallel dimensions `(m, n, k)`, producing a rank-3 result tensor of shape `M x N x K` — because all iterators feed the output through the `linalg.yield`.

assumptions: Standard `linalg.generic` semantics as documented in MLIR Linalg dialect.

questions.subtopic: MLIR / MemRef dialect — strides, memory space, layout
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a strided MemRef type descriptor and understand what its layout affix encodes about memory access patterns.
questions.stem: Consider the MLIR type `memref<4x8xf32, strided<[8, 1], offset: 0>, 3>`. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: A 4×8 column-major FP32 buffer because the second stride is `1`; MLIR's convention is that stride `1` in the last position indicates column-major layout, and the `3` denotes an alignment-in-bytes annotation.
A 4×8 buffer of f32 in memory space 3 (typically GPU shared/workgroup memory), row-major (stride [8, 1]) with offset 0; the element `[i, j]` lives at linear address `i*8 + j` from the base pointer.

A 4×8 buffer whose stride array is contiguous FP32 counts, so element `[i, j]` lives at byte address `i*8*4 + j*4`; the memory-space integer `3` denotes a runtime allocator ID resolved lazily at first access.

A 4×8 tensor value in memory space 3 with a non-standard SSA numbering; the `strided<[8,1], offset:0>` clause is documentation only and does not affect the address computation, which is always row-major for `memref`.

assumptions: MLIR memref strides are in element units unless documented otherwise.
Memory-space integer 3 is a convention used by GPU lowerings for shared memory.

questions.subtopic: MLIR / Operation / Region / Block / Value / Type / Attribute
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the roles of Operation, Region, Block, Value, Type, and Attribute in the MLIR structural model, and identify which entity carries compile-time constants vs. SSA runtime values.
questions.stem: In MLIR's structural model, which statement about Operation, Region, Block, Value, Type, and Attribute is correct?

options.text: Attributes are runtime SSA values attached to an Operation via a special dataflow edge; they can be mutated during execution and are the primary way MLIR represents dynamic scalars inside a Region.

An Operation may contain zero or more Regions; each Region contains one or more Blocks in a CFG; SSA Values flow between Operations at runtime, while Attributes carry compile-time constant metadata attached to an Operation.
A Block is the top-level unit of MLIR IR; each Block owns exactly one Region, and Operations exist inside a Region only as an implementation-level detail invisible to Pass writers.

In MLIR every Value must have both a Type and an Attribute; without the paired Attribute the Type is undefined, which is why `arith.constant` is modelled as a pair `(Type, Attribute)` on a Value edge rather than on the Operation.

assumptions: MLIR core dialect structure as defined in the MLIR LangRef.

questions.subtopic: MLIR / Pass, PassManager, nested pipelines
questions.learningObjective: Reason about MLIR Pass and PassManager semantics: op-scoping, nesting, and how a pass's op-type constrains where it runs.
questions.stem: Which statement about MLIR PassManager and Pass scoping is correct?

options.text: Each Pass declares the Op type it runs on (e.g., `ModuleOp` or `func.func`); the PassManager runs a pass over every matching Op in the IR, and nested pass managers can be composed to run inner passes on inner ops (e.g., a `func.func` pipeline nested inside a `ModuleOp` pipeline).

MLIR Passes are always module-level: any pass registered with the PassManager runs exactly once on the top-level `ModuleOp`, and per-function work is achieved by having the pass walk the module manually with a `walk()` call.
The PassManager runs all registered passes in parallel by default; users must explicitly opt out of parallelism to guarantee ordering, since MLIR provides no sequential pipeline semantics.
Passes may freely modify any op in the IR regardless of the declared scope; the declared Op type is only a documentation hint used by the pass registry to display help text.

assumptions: Standard upstream MLIR PassManager design.

questions.subtopic: MLIR / Pattern Rewrite, greedy driver, canonicalization
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how MLIR pattern rewriting composes rewrite patterns, and identify what canonicalization patterns can and cannot do.
questions.stem: The IR below is fed to the MLIR canonicalization pass with the standard `arith` folder/patterns registered. Which output is correct?

options.text: MLIR canonicalization never removes dead constants; only an explicit DCE pass can eliminate `%c0` and `%c1`, so they will remain in the output IR even after full canonicalization.

The pattern driver applies each canonicalization pattern at most once in source order; if `add-zero` fires before `sub`'s operands are unified, the `sub` cannot be folded and the returned value is `arith.subi %x, %x`.

`add-zero` and `mul-one` are folded, but `sub %x, %x → 0` is a semantic transformation outside the scope of canonicalization, since it changes the SSA def-use chain and thus requires an explicit `-fold-symmetric-ops` pass.

After canonicalization, `add %x, 0` folds to `%x`, `mul %x, 1` folds to `%x`, and `sub %x, %x` folds to `arith.constant 0 : i32`; the function returns a fresh constant zero and both `%c0` and `%c1` become dead and are DCE'd.

assumptions: Standard upstream `arith` dialect canonicalizers are registered.
The canonicalization pass is `-canonicalize` with default settings.

questions.subtopic: MLIR / Tensor, MemRef, Vector types
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish MLIR `tensor`, `memref`, and `vector` types by their semantics (value vs buffer), aliasing model, and role in the lowering pipeline.
questions.stem: Which statements about MLIR `tensor`, `memref`, and `vector` types are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: `tensor` and `memref` are fully interchangeable; the bufferization pass exists only for user convenience since MLIR's runtime executes both types with identical semantics.
`tensor<...>` is a value type with SSA semantics: producers create new logical tensors; there is no in-place mutation and no explicit aliasing between different SSA values.

`memref<...>` models a buffer with an explicit memory space, strides, and offset; multiple `memref` values can alias the same underlying storage, and stores through one memref are visible via aliased memrefs.

`vector<...>` typically models SIMD/SIMT lane-aligned values held in registers; vector types are the primary lowering target for `arith` ops on `tensor` before bufferization, because tensors cannot be lowered to LLVM directly.

assumptions: Upstream MLIR bufferization semantics.
The reader is thinking of built-in tensor/memref/vector types, not downstream extensions.

questions.subtopic: ONNX / Interchange format vs high-performance runtime
questions.learningObjective: Understand the boundary between ONNX as a model interchange format and the runtimes that consume it, avoiding the assumption that interchange = high performance.
questions.stem: Which statements about ONNX as a model interchange format are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: ONNX defines a portable representation of a model (operators, initializers, shapes, versions); it does not itself define how to execute the model efficiently on any specific hardware — that is the job of ONNX-consuming runtimes (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, OpenVINO, IREE, etc.).

Two runtimes consuming the same ONNX model can produce different latency/throughput because their operator implementations, fusion policies, kernel selection, and memory management are runtime-specific, even though the numerical results should match within spec tolerance.
Because ONNX is a widely adopted format, exporting a model to ONNX automatically guarantees it will be as fast on any target as the fastest hand-tuned implementation for that hardware.
ONNX bundles a specific execution engine into the model file; loading an `.onnx` file automatically brings in a runtime and there is no distinction between the format and its executors.

assumptions: ONNX as documented at onnx.ai.

questions.subtopic: ONNX / Operator Set, Opset versioning
questions.learningObjective: Understand ONNX's operator set and opset versioning model.
questions.stem: Which statement about ONNX opsets is correct?

options.text: ONNX opsets are monotonically merged over time: a runtime supporting opset 18 automatically supports the exact semantics of every opset from 1 to 17 without any per-version handling.
ONNX opsets are only a display feature; every ONNX runtime implements the union of all opset versions simultaneously, so opset numbers can be ignored.

An ONNX model declares a specific opset version (e.g., `opset_import: [domain="", version=17]`); each op's semantics is defined by the version listed in that opset, and consumers must implement the exact opset version to execute the model correctly.
The opset version determines only the file-format layout on disk; the operator semantics themselves never change across versions.

assumptions: ONNX specification as of 2026; opset versioning is stable across recent revisions.

questions.subtopic: ONNX / Shape inference — dynamic vs static shapes
questions.learningObjective: Understand ONNX shape inference and how dynamic dimensions are represented in a model.
questions.stem: Which statement about ONNX shape inference and dynamic dimensions is correct?

options.text: ONNX represents dynamic dimensions by encoding a runtime `Tensor<int64>` shape argument as an implicit first input to every op, replacing the static shape annotation.
ONNX shape inference always produces fully static shapes; any op that cannot be statically resolved is deleted from the graph before serialization.
ONNX has no shape inference mechanism; every runtime must implement its own inference from scratch, and the model file never contains any type/shape annotations.

ONNX supports symbolic (named) dynamic dimensions on tensor shapes; `onnx.shape_inference` propagates concrete or symbolic shape/dtype information through the graph where op rules allow it, and unresolved dimensions remain symbolic — consumers use this info for planning but do not require full staticity.

assumptions: ONNX shape inference API and TensorShapeProto as documented.

questions.subtopic: ONNX / Versioning, IR version vs Opset version
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish ONNX's IR version (model format) from opset version (operator semantics).
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes ONNX's IR version from its opset version?

options.text: IR version defines the on-disk protobuf schema/structural features of ModelProto (e.g., which optional fields exist); opset version defines the semantics of individual operators (e.g., what attributes Conv accepts). The two evolve independently, and a model must declare both.
IR version and opset version are two names for the same field; both refer to the operator set used by the model.
IR version is used only during export; runtimes ignore it and only look at the opset when executing.
Opset version is a subset of IR version: opset N is always the operator content of IR version N; both must be equal in every valid ONNX model.

assumptions: ONNX specification distinction between IR version and opset version.

questions.subtopic: StableHLO / Operator set stability and framework/compiler portability
questions.learningObjective: Explain the design goal of StableHLO as a portable operator set between frameworks and compilers.
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the design purpose of StableHLO?

options.text: StableHLO is a hardware-independent runtime that directly executes ML models on GPU/TPU/CPU without invoking any downstream compiler; it replaces XLA at the execution layer.

StableHLO is a versioned operator set with a formal specification that acts as a portability contract between ML frameworks (as producers) and compilers (as consumers), providing forward/backward compatibility guarantees so framework upgrades and compiler upgrades can proceed independently.
StableHLO is a Python DSL for defining new ops in JAX; it is not an IR and cannot be serialized to disk.
StableHLO is a strict subset of TensorFlow's SavedModel format; every StableHLO program is directly a SavedModel and vice versa.

assumptions: OpenXLA StableHLO project design as documented at openxla.org/stablehlo.

questions.subtopic: StableHLO / Framework-compiler portability design intent
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the community invests in a stable, versioned operator set at the framework-compiler boundary.
questions.stem: Which statement best captures the design rationale for putting a stable, versioned operator set (StableHLO) at the framework-compiler boundary?

options.text: It decouples the release cycles of frameworks (PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow) and compilers (XLA, IREE, ...): each side can evolve independently as long as they respect the StableHLO version compatibility contract, avoiding an O(frameworks × compilers) integration matrix and enabling shared optimization work.

It forces every framework to adopt identical implementation details, so any two frameworks that consume StableHLO produce bit-identical outputs on all hardware, eliminating framework-level differences in numerical results.
It replaces the need for framework-specific tracing tools; any framework that emits StableHLO no longer needs its own graph capture mechanism (TorchDynamo, JAX's tracer, TF's tf.function).
It exists primarily to give the compiler backend access to Python source code so that Python-native optimizations (e.g., decorator rewriting) can be applied at the compiler level.

assumptions: OpenXLA StableHLO design motivations as documented.

questions.subtopic: TVM / External library integration — BYOC, extern ops
questions.learningObjective: Understand how TVM integrates external kernel libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN, TensorRT) into a Relax program.
questions.stem: Which statement about how TVM integrates external libraries (e.g., cuBLAS, cuDNN, TensorRT) into a Relax program is correct?

options.text: External library calls are inlined into TensorIR PrimFunc bodies at compile time; the compiler then applies MetaSchedule to tune the library implementation just like any generated code.
TVM cannot call any external library from a compiled Relax program; all compute must be expressed as generated PrimFunc bodies to be executable by the Relax VM.

TVM's Bring-Your-Own-Codegen (BYOC) and extern-op mechanisms let a Relax op be lowered to an opaque call into a target library instead of a generated PrimFunc; the compiler treats such calls as black boxes at fusion and scheduling time but still tracks shapes/dtypes at the graph level.
BYOC only supports CPU targets; GPU external libraries like cuBLAS must be linked at runtime via the host Python interpreter and cannot be encoded into the compiled artifact.

assumptions: Standard TVM Unity BYOC and extern-op flows.

questions.subtopic: TVM / Operator fusion — graph-level and tensor-level
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish graph-level operator fusion in Relax from loop-level fusion in TensorIR and understand what each achieves.
questions.stem: Which statements about operator fusion in TVM are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Graph-level fusion in Relax groups multiple ops into a single fused sub-function (often a call into a fused PrimFunc), reducing kernel launch counts and enabling shared intermediate buffers.

Loop-level fusion in TensorIR (`sch.compute_inline`, `sch.reverse_compute_at`) merges producer and consumer loop nests inside a PrimFunc, eliminating intermediate materialization and improving locality.
Graph-level fusion can always fuse arbitrary op pairs; there is no notion of a fusion boundary or per-op fusion policy in Relax.
External-library ops (e.g., calls to cuBLAS or cuDNN) can be freely fused with generated PrimFunc kernels because Relax's fusion pass rewrites external calls into loop bodies at compile time.

assumptions: Standard TVM Unity fusion pipeline.

questions.subtopic: TVM / MetaSchedule — search-based auto-tuning
questions.learningObjective: Understand the role of MetaSchedule in TVM: search space, measurement, cost model, and its relationship to TensorIR schedule primitives.
questions.stem: Which statement about TVM's MetaSchedule is correct?

options.text: MetaSchedule operates at the Relax graph level; it does not touch loop-level IR and instead selects among pre-built kernel library implementations.

MetaSchedule replaces TensorIR schedule primitives with a purely analytical solver based on the polyhedral model; it does not perform any real measurement and relies solely on integer-linear-programming derived closed-form costs.

MetaSchedule automatically generates candidate schedules over TensorIR PrimFunc using rule-based expansion (space definition), then evaluates them via a cost model and real measurement on target hardware, iterating to find high-performance implementations.
MetaSchedule is deterministic: given the same PrimFunc and target, it always produces the same schedule regardless of search budget, seed, or measurement noise.

assumptions: MetaSchedule as documented for TVM Unity.
Search-based tuning as the intended workflow.

questions.subtopic: TVM / Relax vs Relay — design motivation
questions.learningObjective: Understand what Relax adds relative to Relay and why the TVM community introduced a new graph-level IR.
questions.stem: Which statement best captures the design motivation behind Relax over the older Relay IR in TVM Unity?

options.text: Relax removes the module concept from TVM; unlike Relay's IRModule, Relax programs are flat lists of ops without functions, calls, or nested regions, which simplifies serialization.
Relax's main goal is to replace TensorIR entirely by folding all loop-level scheduling into a single graph IR; PrimFunc is retained only for legacy compatibility.

Relax is a graph-level IR designed to (i) natively support symbolic/dynamic shapes as first-class values, (ii) unify graph-level and tensor-level IRs by cross-calling PrimFunc via TensorIR, and (iii) enable Python-native metaprogramming and staged transformation — capabilities that Relay's typed functional core could not cleanly express.
Relax exists solely to add automatic differentiation to TVM; it does not change how shapes, calls, or tensor programs are represented compared to Relay.

assumptions: TVM Unity / Relax reflects the design goals documented on tvm.apache.org.

questions.subtopic: TVM / TensorIR schedule primitives — split, bind, cache_read
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the effect of individual TensorIR schedule primitives on the resulting loop structure and buffer accesses.
questions.stem: You have a TensorIR PrimFunc computing `C = A + B` with a single loop `for i in range(N)`. Which of the following schedule sequences are consistent with the semantics of TensorIR schedule primitives? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: `sch.vectorize(loop=i)` is guaranteed to succeed on any loop regardless of the loop's extent, alignment, or the underlying target; TensorIR will silently emit scalar code if vectorization is impossible.

`sch.bind(loop=i, thread_axis='threadIdx.x')` may be applied without any prior split; this is a valid legalization that turns a single serial loop into a per-thread compute where each thread handles one element and blockDim is set to the loop's extent.

`sch.split(loop=i, factors=[None, 256])` produces two nested loops `(io, ii)` with `ii` size 256 and `io` size `ceildiv(N, 256)`; then `sch.bind(io, 'blockIdx.x')` and `sch.bind(ii, 'threadIdx.x')` map the two loops to the CUDA launch grid, producing a canonical vector-add kernel.

`sch.cache_read(block='C', read_buffer_index=0, storage_scope='shared')` inserts a shared-memory staging buffer between the load of `A` and its use in the C block, without changing the mathematical result.

assumptions: Standard TensorIR schedule primitive semantics as documented.
The reader is thinking of Unity-era TensorIR (not the pre-Unity TE `create_schedule` API).

questions.subtopic: TVM / TensorIR PrimFunc — compute + schedule separation
questions.learningObjective: Explain how TensorIR represents tensor-level programs and how compute and schedule are separated.
questions.stem: Which statement about TVM TensorIR PrimFunc is correct?

options.text: TensorIR schedule primitives are semantic transformations that may change the mathematical result of the PrimFunc; users must supply a separate golden reference to verify correctness after each schedule step.
A PrimFunc is a graph-level op description without loops; all loop structure lives in Relax and is projected into PrimFunc only during code generation.

A PrimFunc is a loop-level tensor program with explicit blocks, iteration variables, and buffer accesses; schedule primitives (`split`, `tile`, `bind`, `vectorize`) transform the loop structure without changing the underlying compute semantics.
PrimFunc bodies are opaque Python callables that TVM's runtime interprets at execution time; TVM does not analyze or transform their internal structure at compile time.

assumptions: TensorIR as documented in TVM Unity docs.
Schedule primitives operate on the block/loop structure.

questions.subtopic: TVM / Relax VM runtime — dynamic execution model
questions.learningObjective: Understand the role of the Relax VM in executing compiled TVM programs and its position relative to static compilation.
questions.stem: Which statement about the Relax VM in TVM is correct?

options.text: The Relax VM only supports CPU targets; GPU execution in TVM is handled by a separate compile-time-only pipeline that emits standalone `.so` files without any VM involvement.

The Relax VM is a Python interpreter that parses and executes Relax IR line-by-line at runtime; it does not require any AOT compilation of PrimFuncs, and switching to a different target only requires changing an environment variable.
The Relax VM eliminates the need for a compiler: it JIT-compiles TensorIR at every function call, so the entire tuning + scheduling pipeline runs at inference time.

The Relax VM is a bytecode-based runtime that executes a compiled Relax program: it dispatches PrimFunc calls, external-library calls, and control flow, and it handles dynamic-shape allocation and object lifetime — enabling static compilation of graph structure with runtime resolution of dynamic dimensions.

assumptions: Relax VM design as documented in TVM Unity.

questions.subtopic: XLA / Buffer assignment, aliasing, in-place operations
questions.learningObjective: Understand XLA's buffer assignment: value → buffer mapping, aliasing, and how in-place execution is decided.
questions.stem: Which statement about XLA's buffer assignment pass is correct?

options.text: XLA's buffer assignment maps HLO SSA values to physical buffers, allowing values with disjoint liveness to share the same buffer and enabling in-place execution when the compiler can prove the input value is no longer needed after the operation.
Buffer assignment gives each HLO value its own dedicated buffer for the lifetime of the program; buffer reuse only happens at runtime through the memory allocator.
Buffer assignment is a runtime pass executed on every step of the model; it is not part of static compilation and produces different assignments each iteration.
HLO ops are always executed out-of-place; XLA does not support in-place semantics for any operation, so all elementwise updates must allocate a fresh buffer.

assumptions: Standard XLA buffer assignment as documented in the OpenXLA project.

questions.subtopic: XLA / Fusion — kinds and boundaries
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the kinds of fusion XLA performs (loop, input, output) and their motivations.
questions.stem: Which statements about XLA's operator fusion are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: XLA distinguishes multiple fusion kinds (e.g., 'loop' fusion, 'input' fusion, 'output' fusion) chosen based on producer/consumer memory-access patterns, so that fused kernels avoid materializing intermediate tensors when the access pattern is compatible.

Elementwise ops chained with reductions can be output-fused into the reduction kernel so the elementwise stage runs inside the reduction's inner loop and no intermediate tensor is written to global memory.
XLA always fuses any two adjacent ops in the HLO graph; fusion has no cost model and no boundaries, so producer/consumer pairs are unconditionally combined into one kernel.
Fusion in XLA operates by cloning the producer's HLO source into the consumer's IR file at compile time; there is no compiler-side representation of a fused kernel, only a copy at the string level.

assumptions: XLA fusion pass as documented; naming may evolve but the taxonomy is stable.

questions.subtopic: XLA / Static vs dynamic shape handling
questions.learningObjective: Understand XLA's static-shape orientation and how dynamic shape is handled (bucketing, dynamic dims, StableHLO dynamic ops).
questions.stem: Which statements about static vs dynamic shape handling in XLA / StableHLO are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: StableHLO includes `dynamic_*` ops (e.g., `dynamic_reshape`, `dynamic_slice`, `real_dynamic_slice`) that let programs represent computations whose shapes depend on runtime values without requiring re-compilation for every value.
XLA achieves dynamic-shape support by removing all shape annotations from HLO; static shapes are only used for debug logging and are not required by any optimization pass.
Serving systems using XLA often mitigate re-compilation cost by shape bucketing / padding: routing many similar shapes to a small fixed set of pre-compiled shape configurations.

XLA is fundamentally static-shape-oriented: each HLO computation is specialized for concrete shapes at compile time, so shape changes typically trigger a fresh compilation (potentially very costly if unbounded).

assumptions: XLA / StableHLO static-first orientation as documented.

questions.subtopic: XLA SPMD / GSPMD — sharding annotations and automatic parallelization
questions.learningObjective: Understand the basic idea of XLA SPMD partitioning and how sharding annotations drive automatic parallelization.
questions.stem: Which statement about XLA SPMD partitioning (GSPMD) is correct?

options.text: GSPMD replaces the single HLO program with N distinct per-device programs (one per device); each program is compiled and shipped independently, and there is no shared HLO representation after partitioning.

GSPMD takes an HLO program annotated with sharding specifications (e.g., `sharding={devices=[4,1] ...}` on some tensors) and rewrites it into a per-device program that runs the same computation on each device, inserting collective communication (all-reduce/all-gather/reshard) where required to preserve semantics.
GSPMD partitions only the model parameters; activations are always fully replicated across devices, so it does not require any collective communication for forward or backward passes.
GSPMD is a runtime-only system; sharding annotations are ignored by the compiler and interpreted by the XLA runtime scheduler, which decides sharding decisions per step based on load.

assumptions: GSPMD as described in the XLA / OpenXLA project and Xu et al. 2021 paper.
